claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Cansa'yapi: community continuity and public history
claimBlocks.text: The Lower Sioux Indian Community identifies its members as Mdewakanton Dakota and calls its Minnesota River homeland Cansa'yapi. Its account describes families returning despite exile. A companion historic-site page dates tribal management of the Lower Sioux Agency site to 2007. Together these pages connect community continuity with authority to interpret a place shaped by federal reservation policy.

The SMSC identifies itself as a Dakota government within the Oceti Ṡakowiŋ, alongside related Dakota, Lakota and Nakota peoples. Its public timeline follows forced removal, later land purchases and its own 1969 governmental organization. The community dates Hoċokata Ṫi's opening to 2019. These are a particular Mdewakanton government's institutions, not a model shared by every Dakota community.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Prairie Island's account of land and persistence
claimBlocks.text: Prairie Island identifies its members as Bdewakantunwan, or Mdewakanton, Eastern Dakota. Its history follows families who remained or returned, purchased land and maintained a community despite displacement. The Tribe also describes pressures from dam construction, a nuclear generating plant and rail transport. These concerns are its situated account of Prairie Island, rather than a general description of every Dakota homeland.

Dakota Wicohan traces its origins to a 2001 language team involving Upper Sioux, Lower Sioux and Twin Cities Dakota, followed by nonprofit incorporation in 2002. Its account connects intergenerational language learning, teacher preparation and outreach with community relationships. This educational organization works across political boundaries; it is not another tribal government. Its undated speaker and program totals are not current measurements.

MNHS describes noncombatant Dakota imprisonment at Fort Snelling during 1862–1863 and forced transport to Crow Creek in May 1863. It distinguishes congressional actions of February 16 and March 3, 1863, concerning treaty annulment and removal. Its account also discusses a separate Ho-Chunk expulsion. These histories should not be conflated or taken to mean every Dakota person participated in the war.

claimBlocks.text: The Mendota treaty text names Mdewakanton and Wahpekute parties, rather than every Dakota community. Its published version records a land cession, differentiated payments and funding for education and farms. It also marks Article 3 as deleted and prints supplemental terms. This specific written federal record does not establish fully informed consent, oral understandings, promise fulfillment or present individual entitlements.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Four Minnesota governments within wider Dakota peoples
claimBlocks.text: MnDOT's public inventory names Lower Sioux, Prairie Island, Shakopee Mdewakanton and Upper Sioux as Minnesota Dakota communities. Each government needs its own institutional reading. This four-government inventory is a Minnesota access point, not an exhaustive list of Dakota peoples or their communities elsewhere in the United States and Canada.

integrationNotes: Preserve exact original p95-s1, p95-s2 and p95-s3 IDs and URLs. New sources do not replace provenance. Both teaching-kit versions count as one conservative work family and currently contribute zero substantive works; Black Hills paper is contextual, not a Minnesota Dakota government source.

Six new substantive units: one Lower Sioux public account collection, one SMSC public account collection, Prairie Island history, Dakota Wicohan organizational/language account, MNHS historical account and actual Mendota treaty text. Supporting MnDOT inventory adds no substantive count.

The old Black Hills card was labeled Indigenous-led. Actual page authorship identifies a student legal paper; the proposed type is Academic / reference with detailed sourceKind and explicit authority limits, without asserting peer review or verified representative Indigenous government authorship.

The existing two-section source guide should be rewritten with the supplied scoped sections. Its generic assertion about broader people/language identity should not remain solely backed by a partially read broad South Dakota kit.

Dakota, Lakota and Nakota are related names/peoples in the situated community introduction, not interchangeable governments. This packet does not impose an exhaustive linguistic taxonomy or transfer Ojibwe material to Dakota. Four Minnesota governments are not the entire Dakota people.

Upper Sioux appears through the official inventory and Dakota Wicohan origins, without a direct government history review. Do not write its detailed history from other communities' accounts. Santee Dakota original335 is related reading, not an automatic alias for all four Minnesota governments.

Treaty transcription and later historical/legal summaries are dated evidence, not current legal advice. Separate written wording, deleted/supplemental provisions, community accounts and unreviewed oral understandings.

No new overview is proposed. Recompute full public annotation, scope, subresource scopes and every retained/new cited body plus any overview at integration. Each proposed block is at most 65 words; packet support is deliberately compact.

No further discovery after this saved bounded packet; preserve remaining research gaps for a later authorized window. No original media, traditional motif, audio, ceremony, sensitive site, private family record or access-control bypass.

initialAdequacy.assessment: Useful Minnesota-focused development; broader Dakota coverage remains incomplete
initialAdequacy.limitations: Three Minnesota governments supply direct historical accounts; Upper Sioux institutional history was inaccessible. Language evidence is an organizational self-account, not a grammar, evaluated curriculum or current speaker census. Wider US/Canadian Dakota communities and direct Dakota-authored historical scholarship need future work.

researchGaps: A substantial directly accessible Upper Sioux government history and dated public educational publication remain unreviewed.

Dakota communities outside Minnesota, including particular governments in the Dakotas, Nebraska and Canada, require their own voices and source scopes. This is not an exhaustive homeland or present-community map.
Specialist Dakota language scholarship is needed for precise variants/classification; undated public speaker totals and simplified labels should not become present demographic findings.

Original treaty scans, oral understandings, 1863 statutes, community constitutions and selected Dakota-authored historical scholarship would deepen this initial set. Bibliographic listings and search excerpts are not substitutes for reading them.

Dated education reports and community evaluations would be needed before describing current operations, participation or outcomes. No clinical, legal, membership or service-eligibility conclusion is proposed.
